section.title: Rejection at Nazareth and Ministry in Capernaum
section.sectionRationale: Luke opens Jesus' public ministry with a scene that serves as the keynote for the whole Gospel. In His hometown synagogue Jesus reads Isaiah 61 and announces that its good news to the poor and release to the captive is fulfilled in Him, then warns, by the examples of Elijah and Elisha, that God's grace reaches outsiders. The town's admiration turns to murderous rage. Jesus goes on to Capernaum, where His word carries authority over demons and disease, and He presses on to preach the kingdom because that is why He was sent.
section.thesis: Jesus announces Himself as the Spirit-anointed Servant who brings good news to the poor and freedom to the captive, and though His own town rejects Him for extending God's grace beyond its borders, His word proves to be a word of authority that frees, heals, and cannot be confined.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the return to Galilee in the Spirit's power; the Nazareth manifesto from Isaiah 61; the offense of grace to outsiders and the town's rage; the word of authority over an unclean spirit at Capernaum; and healings at Simon's house and the mission to preach the kingdom everywhere.

units.label: Return in the Spirit's power
units.note: teaching in the synagogues of Galilee

verses.text: Jesus returned to Galilee in the power of the Spirit, and the news about Him spread throughout the surrounding region.
He taught in their synagogues and was glorified by everyone.

units.label: The Nazareth manifesto
units.note: the Spirit of the Lord is on Me

verses.text: Then Jesus came to Nazareth, where He had been brought up. As was His custom, He entered the synagogue on the Sabbath. And when He stood up to read,
the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was handed to Him. Unrolling it, He found the place where it was written:

“The Spirit of the Lord is on Me, because He has anointed Me to preach {{euangelizo|good news}} to the poor. He has sent Me to proclaim {{aphesis|liberty}} to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to release the oppressed,
to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor.”
Then He rolled up the scroll, returned it to the attendant, and sat down. The eyes of everyone in the synagogue were fixed on Him,
and He began by saying, “Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing.”

units.label: The offense of grace to outsiders
units.note: no prophet is accepted in his hometown

verses.text: All spoke well of Him and marveled at the gracious words that came from His lips. “Isn’t this the son of Joseph?” they asked.
Jesus said to them, “Surely you will quote this proverb to Me: ‘Physician, heal yourself! Do here in Your hometown what we have heard that You did in Capernaum.’”
Then He added, “Truly I tell you, no prophet is {{dektos|accepted}} in his hometown.
But I tell you truthfully that there were many widows in Israel in the time of Elijah, when the sky was shut for three and a half years and great famine swept over all the land.
Yet Elijah was not sent to any of them, but to the widow of Zarephath in Sidon.
And there were many lepers in Israel in the time of Elisha the prophet. Yet not one of them was cleansed, only Naaman the Syrian.”
On hearing this, all the people in the synagogue were enraged.
They got up, drove Him out of the town, and led Him to the brow of the hill on which the town was built, in order to throw Him over the cliff.
But Jesus passed through the crowd and went on His way.

units.label: A word of authority at Capernaum
units.note: with authority He commands the unclean spirits

verses.text: Then He went down to Capernaum, a town in Galilee, and on the Sabbath He began to teach the people.
They were astonished at His teaching, because His message had {{exousia|authority}}.
In the synagogue there was a man possessed by the spirit of an unclean demon. He cried out in a loud voice,
“Ha! What do You want with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have You come to destroy us? I know who You are, the Holy One of God!”
But Jesus rebuked the demon. “Be silent!” He said. “Come out of him!” At this, the demon threw the man down before them all and came out without harming him.
All the people were overcome with amazement and asked one another, “What is this message? With authority and power He commands the unclean spirits, and they come out!”
And the news about Jesus spread throughout the surrounding region.

units.label: Healings and the mission to preach
units.note: I must preach the good news of the kingdom

verses.text: After Jesus had left the synagogue, He went to the home of Simon, whose mother-in-law was suffering from a high fever. So they appealed to Jesus on her behalf,
and He stood over her and rebuked the fever, and it left her. And she got up at once and began to serve them.
At sunset, all who were ill with various diseases were brought to Jesus, and laying His hands on each one, He healed them.
Demons also came out of many people, shouting, “You are the Son of God!” But He rebuked the demons and would not allow them to speak, because they knew He was the Christ.
At daybreak, Jesus went out to a solitary place, and the crowds were looking for Him. They came to Him and tried to keep Him from leaving.
But Jesus told them, “I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well, because that is why I was sent.”
And He continued to preach in the synagogues of Judea.

euangelizo.gloss: To announce good news, to proclaim glad tidings. In the Isaiah text Jesus reads, the Anointed One is sent to euangelizo the poor. Luke loves this word; here it names the very heart of Jesus' mission, a gospel first for the humble, the broken, and the outsider.

aphesis.gloss: Release, liberty, forgiveness. The word for freeing prisoners is the same word used for the forgiveness of sins. Isaiah's promise of liberty to captives points beyond political freedom to the deeper release Jesus brings, freedom from sin, guilt, and bondage to evil.

exousia.gloss: Authority, the rightful power to act. The crowds are astonished that Jesus' word carries exousia: He teaches with it and commands unclean spirits with it, and they obey. His authority is not borrowed from the scribes but is His own as the Holy One of God.

dektos.gloss: Acceptable, welcome, favorable. Jesus proclaims the acceptable year of the Lord, the time of God's favor, and then says no prophet is dektos, accepted, in his hometown. The same word frames both the offer of grace and the tragedy of its rejection.

basic.context: Jesus begins His public work in Galilee, teaching in synagogues with growing fame. In Nazareth, His hometown, He reads from Isaiah 61 about the Spirit-anointed Servant who brings good news to the poor and freedom to the captive, and declares that this is fulfilled in Him. When He points out that God once sent Elijah and Elisha to help outsiders rather than Israelites, the crowd turns violent. Jesus moves on to Capernaum, where His word drives out a demon and heals the sick, and He insists on preaching the kingdom everywhere.
basic.hermeneutics: The Nazareth scene is programmatic: Luke places it first to announce the themes of the whole Gospel, good news to the poor, release to captives, and grace that overflows to outsiders. Read the Elijah and Elisha examples as the reason for the rage; the offense is not merely a local prophet but a gospel that reaches beyond the boundaries of the insider. The Capernaum scenes then show the announced liberty happening in real deliverance and healing.
basic.originalLanguages: Jesus is anointed to euangelizo, to bring good news, to the poor, and to proclaim aphesis, release, to captives, the same word used for the forgiveness of sins. He proclaims the dektos, acceptable, year of the Lord, then notes that no prophet is dektos, accepted, at home. In Capernaum His word carries exousia, authority, so that even unclean spirits obey.
basic.typology: Jesus fulfills Isaiah's Servant who preaches the year of the Lord's favor, the true Jubilee. Elijah's mercy to the widow of Zarephath and Elisha's cleansing of Naaman the Syrian foreshadow the gospel reaching the nations. The synagogue rejection anticipates the greater rejection at Jerusalem, and Jesus passing through the murderous crowd foreshadows that His hour is not yet.
basic.christ: Jesus is the Spirit-anointed Messiah of Isaiah 61, the one in whom the year of God's favor dawns. He is the Holy One of God whose word commands demons and disease. He deliberately extends grace beyond the insider and is rejected for it, a rejection that foreshadows the cross, yet He cannot be stopped and presses on to preach the kingdom.
basic.god: God's ancient promise of a Jubilee of release comes true in Jesus. God's grace is shown to be free and sovereign, reaching a Sidonian widow and a Syrian general, not bound by nation or merit. God's word in Jesus carries real authority to free and heal, and God's purpose sends Jesus onward, for that is why He was sent.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 61:1-2 is the text Jesus reads and fulfills. 1 Kings 17 and 2 Kings 5 tell of Elijah and Elisha and the outsiders they blessed. Luke 7:22 echoes the manifesto in Jesus' answer to John. Acts shows the gospel going out to the nations, fulfilling the pattern set here.
basic.oneStory: The year of the Lord's favor has arrived in the person of Jesus, who brings the poor good news and the captive release. His own town rejects the grace that overflows to outsiders, foreshadowing the cross, yet the word of the kingdom will not be silenced. It goes out with authority to free and heal, running ahead toward the nations, exactly as Isaiah promised and Acts will record.

context.literary:
Luke 4:14-44 is built as a triptych with the Nazareth scene as its centre panel. On either side Luke places summaries of success: the news spreads and Jesus is 'glorified by everyone,' verses 14 and 15, and after Capernaum the news spreads again, verse 37. Between them is a scene that begins in praise and ends in an attempted murder, verses 16 to 30. The pattern teaches the reader that popularity is not the measure of the message. The Gospel opens its public ministry with a rejection, and it does not hide it.

Within the Nazareth scene the action moves in four small steps. Jesus stands, reads, sits and speaks, verses 16 to 21, in the posture of a teacher in a synagogue. Luke slows the camera: the scroll is handed, unrolled, found, read, rolled up, returned, and then 'the eyes of everyone in the synagogue were fixed on Him,' verse 20. The silence before the single sentence, 'Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing,' is deliberate. The sermon, as Luke gives it, is one line. The rest of the scene is the audience's reaction, which comes in two waves, wonder in verse 22 and fury in verse 28, separated by Jesus' two sharp replies about the proverb and about Elijah and Elisha.

The reading itself is a collage. Luke gives the opening of Isaiah 61:1-2, but he stops in the middle of verse 2, before 'the day of our God's vengeance,' and he inserts a phrase borrowed from Isaiah 58:6, 'to release the oppressed.' The chosen texts are about freedom and favour, and the point where Jesus stops is part of the story. The part that is left off is not denied; it simply belongs to a later day.

Capernaum then answers Nazareth. Where the hometown demanded signs and rejected grace, the lakeside town is astonished at the teaching and watches the word do what it says. Luke mirrors the two halves with matching words: 'authority' in verse 32 and 'authority and power' in verse 36, 'rebuked' in verses 35, 39 and 41. The chapter closes with the mission statement 'I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God,' verse 43, which echoes the 'preach good news' of verse 18.
context.historical:
The synagogue was the centre of village life in Galilee, a place of reading, teaching, prayer and local business. Luke says that the Sabbath visit was 'His custom,' verse 16, and that He stood to read and sat to teach, which fits the ordinary pattern of a synagogue service. The 'attendant' who handed the scroll was the synagogue officer who looked after the scrolls. Isaiah would have been a large leather or parchment scroll that had to be unrolled by hand, and Luke's phrase 'He found the place' fits that detail.

The Isaiah text had a long shadow. In Leviticus 25 every fiftieth year was a Jubilee, when land returned to its family and slaves went free: 'proclaim liberty in the land for all its inhabitants,' Leviticus 25:10. The words 'liberty' and 'the year of the LORD's favor' were the Jubilee language that Isaiah 61 turned into the promise of a final release. Israel had been exiled and re-settled, and in Jesus' day was under Roman rule with heavy debts and widespread poverty. To hear 'good news to the poor' read aloud in that setting was to hear the end of the Jubilee delayed for centuries being announced at last.

Nazareth was a small village in the hills of lower Galilee, and the people knew Jesus as 'the son of Joseph,' verse 22. Familiarity bred a certain scepticism, for a carpenter's son from the village was an unlikely prophet. The request for the signs 'we have heard that You did in Capernaum' shows rivalry between a hometown and a nearby lakeside town. Luke has not yet described any Capernaum miracles, so he is telling us that Jesus' reputation had run ahead of the narrative.

The examples from Elijah and Elisha would have stung. Zarephath lay in the region of Sidon, the homeland of Jezebel, the queen who had brought Baal worship into Israel, 1 Kings 16:31. Naaman was the commander of the army of Syria, Israel's northern enemy. To say that God sent His prophets to a Sidonian widow and a Syrian commander while Israelite widows and lepers went unhelped was to say that national privilege was no claim on grace. Rage at that suggestion, and the attempt to throw Him from the edge of the hill, is the response of people who believed their election guaranteed their favour.

Capernaum, by contrast, was a busy lakeside town on the northern shore of Galilee, and Jesus 'went down' to it, as the geography requires, from the hill country. Simon's home was there. Luke's readers would have known that the synagogue was where the Sabbath crowds gathered, and a demon's outcry in such a place was a public matter.
context.canonical:
The Nazareth manifesto stands at the junction of two lines of Old Testament hope, the Jubilee of Leviticus 25 and the Servant of Isaiah. Isaiah 61 belongs to the third section of the book, where an anointed one is sent to those who mourn in Zion. Isaiah 42:1-7 had already described a Servant on whom God puts His Spirit, who opens the eyes of the blind and brings prisoners out of the dungeon, and Isaiah 49:8 speaks of 'the time of favor' and 'the day of salvation.' Luke has Jesus take up all of that. Paul quotes the Isaiah 49 line in 2 Corinthians 6:2, 'now is the time of favor; now is the day of salvation,' a sign that the early church heard the same announcement.

The theme of release runs through Luke. His birth narrative speaks of knowledge of salvation 'through the forgiveness of their sins,' Luke 1:77, using the same word that appears twice in the Nazareth reading. John the Baptist preaches repentance 'for the forgiveness of sins,' Luke 3:3. In chapter 7 Jesus answers John's question with the language of Isaiah: 'The blind receive sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the good news is preached to the poor,' Luke 7:22. Peter's summary in Acts speaks of how 'God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power' and went about 'healing all who were oppressed by the devil,' Acts 10:38. Paul's commission in Acts 26:18 draws on the same cluster, opening eyes and giving forgiveness.

The Elijah and Elisha references reach into the books of Kings, and Luke picks them up later. When Jesus raises the widow's son at Nain, the crowd's cry 'A great prophet has appeared among us!' and the detail that Jesus 'gave him back to his mother,' Luke 7:15-16, recall Elijah's act in 1 Kings 17:23.

The rejection of the prophet is a known pattern. 'He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him,' John 1:11. Jesus later says 'it is not admissible for a prophet to perish outside of Jerusalem,' Luke 13:33. And in Acts, Paul tells the synagogue at Antioch that they first had to hear the word and that 'we now turn to the Gentiles,' Acts 13:46. The pattern of Nazareth, the word going first to Israel, being refused, and then going to the nations, becomes the pattern of the whole book of Acts.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke wants his readers to see that the whole story of Jesus is already contained in the first sermon. He chooses to place the Nazareth scene at the opening of the ministry even though, as the mention of Capernaum shows, it may not have been the first thing that Jesus did. The order is for meaning. Here is the content of the gospel in a single text: Spirit, anointing, good news, release, sight, favour. Here is the response it will meet, wonder that turns to rage. And here is the surprise that will shape the second volume, Acts: God's favour is not restricted to the people who assume it is theirs.

The scene was meant to challenge Luke's Jewish readers to receive the Messiah who came to them and to remember that rejection had happened before. It was also meant to reassure Gentile readers. The widow from Sidon and the commander from Syria are the first outsiders to be named in the Gospel as recipients of God's mercy, and Theophilus and every non-Jewish reader after him can find a place in that line.

Luke also wanted the reader to ask where he stands. 'Today' is a favourite word in his Gospel, and here it presses the question of the hearers. The synagogue had heard the Scripture and admired the speaker, but the issue was whether they would receive the one the Scripture announced. The scene invites the same decision today.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The scene describes what Jesus announced and how Nazareth reacted. It does not command believers to read Isaiah in synagogues or to declare a literal Jubilee in the land. Nor does it tell us that every rejection is a mark of faithfulness. Luke records an attempt to kill the Lord, and he does not suggest that anyone who is disliked is thereby a prophet. The woes of the chapter that follows warn against that conclusion.

What carries forward is the character of the mission. The church that follows Jesus is sent in the same Spirit to the same people: the poor, the captive, the blind, the oppressed. The same Lord who said 'I must preach the good news' said 'As the Father has sent Me, I am sending you,' John 20:21. Believers are to care for the bodily need of the poor and the freedom of the captive, and they are to announce the forgiveness that is the deepest release. They are also warned about their own temptation. It is easy to treat grace as a possession of the insiders, and the story of Elijah and Elisha tells us that a church that bars the door against outsiders is repeating Nazareth.

Another point is about the reading of Scripture. Jesus does not read the verse and leave it as a lesson for the congregation to apply. He declares that it has found its fulfilment in Him, a way of reading that centres on Him. Believers are meant to read the Old Testament as Jesus did, as a book that speaks of Him, Luke 24:27.

debates.question: Who are 'the poor' in verse 18?

views.label: The materially poor
views.case: Luke's Gospel pays steady attention to money and need. Mary sings that the hungry are filled and the rich sent away empty, Luke 1:53, and the woes of Luke 6:24-25 fall on the rich and well fed. The Jubilee background concerns debts, land and release from bondage, and the manifesto's mention of captives and the oppressed has a plainly social reach.

views.label: The spiritually poor
views.case: In Isaiah 61 the poor are those who mourn in Zion and whose spirit is in despair, Isaiah 61:3, and the same Gospel shows Jesus bringing good news to tax collectors and sinners whose poverty was spiritual. Matthew's parallel says 'poor in spirit,' Matthew 5:3. On this view the poor are those who know they have nothing to offer God.

views.label: Both together
views.case: In the Old Testament the poor are often those who are both economically needy and dependent on God because no one else will defend them. The book of Psalms uses the poor as a name for the faithful who wait on the LORD. Luke shows Jesus caring for hunger and sickness while offering forgiveness to those who know their need.

debates.bearing: The third reading fits Luke best. Luke does not spiritualise away real poverty, and he does not treat money as the whole problem. The good news reaches those who have nothing to bring, in body or in spirit, and it calls the better off to share what they have, as Luke 3:11 and 6:30 say.

debates.question: How should we read the crowd's first response in verse 22?

views.label: Genuine admiration that turns
views.case: Luke says that all 'spoke well of Him and marveled at the gracious words,' verse 22. The sudden change in verse 28 would then be driven by Jesus' words about the proverb and about Elijah and Elisha, which exposed the limit of their welcome.

views.label: Ambivalent astonishment
views.case: The remark 'Isn't this the son of Joseph?' can be read as wonder, but also as doubt: how can a local man speak with such authority? Jesus' answer in verse 23 says that He knows they will demand miracles for themselves. On this reading the crowd's wonder was shaped by self-interest from the start.

views.label: A hostile undertone from the beginning
views.case: Some read the verb translated 'spoke well' more cautiously, as bearing witness to Him in a way that already held Him at a distance, and see 'son of Joseph' as the first note of offence. Jesus' ready knowledge of what they will say fits an audience He knew was not trusting.

debates.bearing: Whichever view is taken, the lesson is the same. Admiring Jesus is not the same as receiving Him, and a person can be moved by the gracious words and still turn on the one who speaks them when grace refuses to stay within familiar limits.

study.originalLanguages:
The word 'today,' semeron, is the first word in Jesus' sermon and one of Luke's signature words. It marks the arrival of salvation in the narrative: 'today in the city of David a Savior has been born,' Luke 2:11, 'today salvation has come to this house,' Luke 19:9, and at the cross, 'today you will be with Me in Paradise,' Luke 23:43. Each of those lines turns a promise into a present reality, and the Nazareth 'today' stands at the head of them. The verb 'is fulfilled' is in the perfect tense, which describes an action completed with a result that continues. The promise has not only been spoken but stands fulfilled before their eyes.

The word translated 'liberty' in verse 18 and 'release' in the same verse is the same Greek noun, aphesis. It is Luke's word for forgiveness of sins, as in Luke 1:77 and 3:3, and also the word that stands for release from debt and captivity. The Septuagint uses the same word for the Jubilee, so that the hearers could hear the two meanings together. The good news is a release that works at every level, from the debts of the poor to the debts of the soul.

The 'gracious words' of verse 22 are literally 'words of grace,' with the noun charis. The phrase can describe words that are charming, or words that are about grace, or words that bring it, and Luke may intend all three. Jesus' very next remark shows how the grace will go beyond the audience's limits. The wonder at the words is a response to their style, while the rage in verse 28 is a response to their content.

The proverb 'Physician, heal yourself' is called a parable, parabole, in verse 23. The word means a comparison or a saying that carries a challenge. The crowd's demand is that He prove Himself in His hometown first, and the force of the saying is that charity begins at home. Jesus' reply uses a strong formula, 'Truly I tell you,' with the word amen, which marks a solemn declaration. It is a way of speaking that belongs to Jesus in the Gospels, since prophets announce 'thus says the LORD,' while He says 'amen, I tell you.'

The verb 'rebuked,' epitimao, runs through the chapter. Jesus rebukes the demon in verse 35, the fever in verse 39 and the demons again in verse 41. The word is the language of a commander who speaks to a power and is obeyed, and Luke uses it again when Jesus rebukes the wind and the waves, Luke 8:24. The command to the demon, 'Be silent,' is from a verb that literally means to muzzle. In the same verse the demon is told 'Come out of him,' and obeys. The woman with the fever is treated with the same verb, as though the illness was a hostile power. Luke sees all of the bondage in the world as part of the one domain that the Messiah has come to break.

The woman's response in verse 39 is that she 'began to serve them.' The verb is diakoneo, and it is in a form that shows a continuing activity. Her healing is not an end in itself but sets her free to serve, and the same verb is used of Jesus Himself, who says 'I am among you as one who serves,' Luke 22:27.

Finally, in verse 43 Jesus says 'I must,' using the small Greek word dei that Luke uses for divine necessity. It appears again when the Son of Man 'must suffer many things,' Luke 9:22, and when Jesus says that the Christ had to suffer and enter His glory, Luke 24:26. Jesus' reason, 'because that is why I was sent,' uses the verb apostello, the same verb that appears in verse 18, 'He has sent Me.' The sending in Isaiah and the sending in verse 43 are one.

typology.fulfillment: Every fiftieth year slaves went free, debts were cancelled and land returned to its family, Leviticus 25:10. The institution was a picture of a larger release that Israel's history never fully delivered, and Isaiah 61 promised it again. Jesus declares 'today' that the true Jubilee is here, and the release is aimed at sin, sickness and demonic oppression as well as debt. Paul says that 'now is the day of salvation,' 2 Corinthians 6:2. The type falls short because the Old Testament Jubilee returned property to people who would soon lose it again, while Christ's release is the beginning of an inheritance that cannot be lost, 1 Peter 1:4.

typology.type: Elijah and the widow of Zarephath, 1 Kings 17
typology.fulfillment: Elijah is sent not to Israel's widows but to a widow in Sidon, and her jar of flour and her son's life are preserved, 1 Kings 17:9 and 17:23. Jesus uses the story to show that God's mercy can pass over the privileged to reach the outsider. The pattern comes into focus in Acts, where the gospel crosses boundaries to Samaritans and Gentiles, Acts 8:5 and 10:44-48. Where Elijah's mercy reached one widow in a famine, Jesus' mission reaches the nations. The correspondence limits itself to the principle of free mercy, since Elijah's miracle was a sign and Jesus brings the final salvation.

A foreign commander with a skin disease was cleansed when he humbled himself and dipped in the Jordan, 2 Kings 5:14, while the lepers of Israel were not healed. In the Gospel the cleansing of lepers becomes one of the signs of the Messiah, Luke 7:22, and the cleansing of a Samaritan leper is singled out in Luke 17:15-18. The type shows that the barrier is not nationality but pride. The escalation is that what the Jordan did once for one man, the Messiah's word does for all who come, and it cleanses from sin as well as disease.

The prophets of Israel were regularly refused by their own people, and Jesus names the pattern in verse 24 and again in Luke 13:33-34. The scene at Nazareth previews the larger rejection at Jerusalem, where the crowd that had shouted for Him would cry out for His death. John says 'He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him,' John 1:11. There is an irony in the fact that Jesus 'passed through the crowd' at Nazareth, verse 30, since His hour was not yet. The type goes beyond the prophets who were killed, for this rejected one rises on the third day, Luke 24:7.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ by the first thing He does, which is to read about Himself. When He says 'Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing,' He claims that the Spirit-anointed figure of Isaiah 61 is Himself. The word 'Christ' means the anointed one, and Luke has just shown the anointing at the Jordan, Luke 3:22, where the Holy Spirit descended on Him. Peter later puts the two together: 'God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power,' Acts 10:38. The sermon at Nazareth is the interpretation of that baptism: the anointing was for this mission.

It leads to Christ as the bringer of release. Every item in the reading is something He goes on to do in Luke. He preaches good news to the poor, and sinners and outcasts gather to hear Him. He frees captives, as the man in the synagogue is freed from the unclean spirit. He gives sight to the blind, Luke 18:35-43. He releases the oppressed, as the woman bent over for eighteen years is released, Luke 13:10-17. The deepest of these is forgiveness, because the word for liberty is also the word for forgiveness. Jesus' power over demons and disease is the visible sign of a power over sin.

It leads to Christ as the Holy One of God, whom the demons recognise at once, verse 34. Their confession is true, but He silences it, verse 41. He will not take His testimony from the powers that oppose Him, and He does not want a title shouted before the mission is finished. The demons call Him the Son of God, and verse 41 says that 'they knew He was the Christ.' He accepts the truth of the words and rejects the speakers.

It leads to Christ as the one who is rejected in the pattern of the prophets and who goes on. Nazareth's rage foreshadows the cross, and the line 'But Jesus passed through the crowd and went on His way,' verse 30, is a quiet marker that His death will come at the time He chooses and not before. Luke 9:51 says that He 'resolutely set out for Jerusalem,' and Luke 22:53 says that the hour of the powers of darkness has come. In verse 43 He says 'I must preach the good news,' and later He says that the Son of Man 'must suffer many things,' Luke 9:22. These are the same sense of purpose: the mission is given by the Father and He is on His way.

It leads to Christ as the one who bears what He heals. Matthew quotes Isaiah 53:4 of His healings in Capernaum, 'He took on our infirmities and carried our diseases,' Matthew 8:17, linking them to the Servant who would suffer. The release He announces costs Him something. The good news to the poor is paid for by One who became poor.

It also shows His sympathy for outsiders. Naaman and the widow were not in the line of privilege, and Jesus reaches for them. A reading that stays honest will not say that the Sidonian widow is a code for the church or that the cliff is a code for the cross. The links rest on what Luke himself draws out: the anointing, the mission, the pattern of rejection and the grace that overflows to the nations, Acts 13:46.
study.god:
This passage shows God as the God of release. Whatever binds, whether debt, sickness, demonic power or guilt, God is at work to loosen it. The announcement is not a general wish but a declaration that the time has come, and Luke expresses it as something God does by His Spirit through His anointed. The same God who delivered Israel from slavery in Egypt and who told Israel to keep a Jubilee is the God who sends His Son to do it at last. His character is shown by what He sends: good news to the poor, not a demand to the rich.

It shows God's freedom in grace. The examples of the Sidonian widow and the Syrian commander are not accidents. The LORD sent His prophet to a foreign widow in the very years when many Israelite widows were in need, 1 Kings 17:9, and He cleansed a Syrian when He passed over the lepers of Israel. God is under no obligation to do for one people what He does for another, and no one has a claim on Him. Paul will argue the same point at length in Romans 9 to 11. That freedom is offensive to those who think they have earned a place, and it is a comfort to those who know they have not.

It shows God's authority over the unseen world. The demon in the synagogue knows who Jesus is, and he knows that the confrontation means his end. The word of Jesus is enough: 'Be silent! Come out of him!' There is no ritual and no struggle, only a command. Luke records that the demon threw the man down and 'came out without harming him,' verse 35. God's rule over the spirits is complete, and it is also merciful, since the man is left unharmed.

It shows God's patience and His purposes. The Father's will is that the good news be heard in many towns, and Jesus leaves a place where He is popular, verse 42, because the mission has a shape that crowds do not set. He prays in a solitary place, a pattern Luke notes elsewhere, Luke 5:16. The God of Luke's Gospel works through a Son who depends on Him in prayer. The sending of the Son is also the work of the Spirit, who is the one who anoints, and so verse 18 holds the Father who sends, the Son who is sent and the Spirit who rests on Him.

It shows God's holiness and nearness together. The demon's 'Holy One of God' is a title for the one set apart for God, and the unclean cannot stand before Him. Yet the same Holy One goes to Simon's house and stands over a woman with a fever. Holiness in Jesus does not retreat from need but drives out what defiles.

For worship, this passage gives reason to praise a God who brings release and who is not limited by our assumptions about who deserves it. It also asks for honesty: Nazareth heard the gracious words and then resisted the grace. Worship that is true welcomes the God who goes beyond our boundaries, and does not ask Him to heal us first and keep the outsiders out.

crossReferences.note: The text Jesus reads, set in its original context. The anointed one is sent to bind up the brokenhearted, comfort mourners and give a crown of beauty for ashes. Jesus stops after 'the year of the LORD's favor,' leaving 'the day of vengeance' unread, and the rest of the passage shows what the favour is meant to do.

The phrase 'to set the oppressed free' is borrowed from here and spliced into the reading. The passage describes the fast the LORD chooses, breaking the chains of wickedness and untying the cords of the yoke. Luke's Jesus joins the Servant of Isaiah 61 with the call for true justice in Isaiah 58.

The law of the Jubilee behind the word 'liberty.' Every fiftieth year land returned to its families and the enslaved were set free. Isaiah took the idea as a picture of final release, and Jesus announces that the real Jubilee has begun in His own person.

The story of Elijah and the widow of Zarephath, in Sidon. A foreign widow shares her last food with the prophet and her dead son is restored. Jesus uses it to show that God's mercy had already gone beyond Israel's borders, which is why the synagogue crowd was offended.

The healing of Naaman the Syrian. A commander of Israel's enemy is cleansed by washing in the Jordan after being told to by the prophet, and his flesh becomes like a child's. Jesus points out that many Israelite lepers were not healed, and the point is that God's grace is free and not confined to one nation.

John the Baptist asks whether Jesus is the one who is to come. Jesus answers with the signs of Isaiah, the blind receiving sight and the good news preached to the poor. It is the Nazareth manifesto seen from the other side: the works that Jesus has done are the evidence that the promised Servant has come.

Jesus says a prophet cannot perish outside Jerusalem and mourns over the city that kills the prophets. The refusal at Nazareth is a small version of what will happen there, and the rage of a village anticipates the rage of the capital.

The parallel account of the synagogue at Capernaum. A very similar scene and the same cry 'the Holy One of God' appear, and the astonishment is at a new teaching with authority. Reading it beside Luke shows how deeply the first witnesses were struck by the combination of word and power.

Matthew's account of Simon's mother-in-law and the healings at evening ends by quoting Isaiah 53:4. This links the healings at Capernaum with the Servant who bears sickness, and shows that the release announced at Nazareth is carried through the one who suffers.

Peter summarises the ministry that began in Galilee, saying God anointed Jesus with the Holy Spirit and power and that He went about healing those oppressed by the devil. It reads as a short commentary on Luke 4, and Peter says it to a Gentile household, which is exactly the outward movement Jesus foretold at Nazareth.

Paul tells the Jerusalem crowd that the Lord sent him far away to the Gentiles, and they listen until that word and then demand his death. The rage of Nazareth over mercy to outsiders is repeated in the temple courts, showing that the offence of Luke 4:25-28 never went away.

John states the whole pattern in a sentence: the one through whom the world was made came to His own, and His own did not receive Him, but those who received Him were given the right to become children of God. Nazareth is the first scene in Luke where the sentence comes true.

study.oneStory:
The story of the Bible is a story of captivity and freedom. Adam's rebellion in the garden led to exile, Genesis 3:24, and Israel's story is a long series of captivities and returns: Egypt, the exile in Babylon, and then foreign rule in the land itself. The law's Jubilee and Isaiah's promise of the anointed one both pointed to a time when God would set everything right. By the time of Luke 4 the nation has waited for centuries, and the promise has lost its sharpness. The question the whole Old Testament leaves hanging is who will do it. At Nazareth, the answer is given in the first words of Jesus' ministry.

The scene answers what came before by announcing that the waiting is over. The Spirit who hovered over the waters, who filled the prophets and who was promised for the last days now rests on one man. The anointed Servant of Isaiah, whose mission was always bigger than Israel, has appeared. Its release is at once physical, social and spiritual, because the fall damaged all three.

It also sets up what follows. The turn from praise to fury shows that the new thing will not be received by everyone, and the references to the Sidonian widow and the Syrian commander set the shape of the rest of Luke and the whole of Acts. The gospel will go to the Jew first and then to the Gentile, Romans 1:16, and the pattern of the refusal of the insiders and the welcome of the outsiders will be repeated from Antioch to Rome. The Capernaum scenes show the release in action, as a man is freed, a woman is raised from her fever and the sick are brought at sunset and healed, and Jesus presses on because the work has to be done in other towns too.

It anticipates the cross. The first sermon ends with an attempt on His life, and the last chapters of Luke bring Him to Jerusalem where the attempt succeeds. Isaiah's Servant would heal by bearing our infirmities, Isaiah 53:4, and the release that Jesus proclaims is won by His death and resurrection. What He declared in the synagogue He accomplishes at the cross, where debts are cancelled and the powers are disarmed, Colossians 2:14-15.

The new creation is the full Jubilee. The poor are given the kingdom, the mourners are comforted, and the blind see. 'He will wipe away every tear from their eyes,' Revelation 21:4, and the nations are gathered in, Revelation 7:9. The synagogue that tried to throw Jesus over the cliff is answered by a multitude from every nation, and the favour of the LORD, which Nazareth thought belonged to itself, has no boundary.

sermon.title: This Scripture Is Fulfilled
sermon.why: Preaching Luke 4:16-30, Begg shows Jesus proclaiming Himself the long-awaited Messiah in His hometown synagogue and the crowd's turn to rage, pressing the point that there are only two responses to Jesus, to bow before Him or to reject Him. A faithful, expository handling of the manifesto at the heart of this movement.

quiz.q: What did Jesus claim when He read from Isaiah in the Nazareth synagogue?

options.text: That the Spirit-anointed Servant who brings good news to the poor and release to captives was fulfilled in Him that very day.
options.note: In verse 21 Jesus says, Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing, applying Isaiah 61 to Himself.

options.text: That the prophecy of Isaiah would one day be fulfilled by the Messiah.
options.note: True of Isaiah's promise, but Jesus' startling claim was that it was fulfilled today, in Him, not merely someday.

options.text: That He admired Isaiah as a great prophet of the past.
options.note: He did far more than admire Isaiah; He announced Himself as the fulfillment of the prophecy.

options.text: That the passage applied only to the nation's political freedom.
options.note: The release Jesus proclaims is deeper than politics, the liberty of forgiveness and the year of the Lord's favor.

quiz.q: Why did the people of Nazareth become enraged?

options.text: Because Jesus showed that God's grace, through Elijah and Elisha, reached outsiders like the widow of Zarephath and Naaman the Syrian.
options.note: Their fury flares in verses 25 to 28 when Jesus names Gentiles as recipients of God's mercy.

options.text: Because Jesus refused to perform miracles in His hometown as He had in Capernaum.
options.note: That demand is part of the friction, but the rage erupts specifically at the examples of grace to outsiders.

options.text: Because they could not believe the carpenter's son could read Scripture.
options.note: They marveled at His gracious words; it was the message of grace to outsiders, not His literacy, that enraged them.

options.text: Because Jesus openly denied being the Messiah.
options.note: The opposite: He announced that Isaiah's promise was fulfilled in Him.

quiz.q: What amazed the people of Capernaum about Jesus?

options.text: That His word carried such authority that even unclean spirits obeyed His command.
options.note: Verses 32 and 36 stress the authority of His teaching and His command over demons.

options.text: That He was a compelling and eloquent speaker.
options.note: His words were gracious, but Luke's point is the authority behind them, not mere eloquence.

options.text: That He performed tricks to entertain the crowd.
options.note: These were genuine deliverances and healings, not entertainment or tricks.

options.text: That He taught exactly like the other scribes.
options.note: The contrast is precisely that His teaching had an authority the scribes lacked.

quiz.q: Why did Jesus leave the crowds who wanted Him to stay in Capernaum?

options.text: Because He was sent to preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well.
options.note: Verse 43 gives His reason: that is why He was sent.

options.text: Because He needed rest from the demands of the crowds.
options.note: He did withdraw to pray, but the stated reason for leaving was His mission to preach elsewhere.

options.text: Because the people of Capernaum had rejected Him.
options.note: They wanted Him to stay; He left not from rejection but for the sake of the wider mission.

options.text: Because His work of preaching was finished.
options.note: His work was only beginning; He left to extend it to other towns.

quiz.q: What does the reach of God's grace to Zarephath and Naaman reveal about Jesus' mission?

options.text: That the good news is for the poor and the outsider, not for insiders only, pointing ahead to the nations.
options.note: Jesus' examples announce a gospel that overflows every boundary, fulfilled as the church goes to the Gentiles.

options.text: That God sometimes helps foreigners as well as His own people.
options.note: True but understated; Jesus makes this the very pattern of His mission, not an occasional exception.

options.text: That Israel had been entirely replaced and cast off.
options.note: Jesus is Israel's Messiah offering grace to all; the point is inclusion of outsiders, not the rejection of Israel.

options.text: That grace must be earned by the deserving.
options.note: The widow and the Syrian were undeserving outsiders; the point is grace freely given, not earned.

questions: Jesus announced good news for the poor, the captive, the blind, and the oppressed. Where in your life do you most need to hear that His good news is for the weak and not only the strong?
The people of Nazareth loved Jesus until His grace reached beyond their borders. Is there a group of outsiders whose welcome into God's family you find hard to celebrate?
Jesus said, 'Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing.' What would it mean to receive Him today rather than admiring Him at a safe distance?
The word of Jesus carried authority to free the possessed and heal the sick. Where do you need to trust that His word still has authority over what binds you?
Jesus pressed on to other towns because that is why He was sent. How does His sense of mission challenge your own sense of purpose and calling?

translationNotes.note: Jesus reads from Isaiah 61:1-2 in the Greek Septuagint, which speaks of recovery of sight to the blind. The BSB footnote notes that some manuscripts add to heal the brokenhearted after the poor, filling out the Isaiah text; Luke's reading still names the good news to the poor as central.

The year of the Lord's favor can also be rendered the acceptable year of the Lord. It draws on the year of Jubilee, Leviticus 25, when captives were freed and debts released, now fulfilled in the salvation Jesus brings. Jesus stops the reading before Isaiah's next line about the day of vengeance, leaving the accent on grace.

Leper and leprosy in Scripture cover a range of serious skin diseases, not only the condition called leprosy today, as the BSB footnote explains with reference to Leviticus 13. Naaman the Syrian was a Gentile military commander cleansed by grace, 2 Kings 5.

The BSB reads the synagogues of Judea, while some manuscripts read Galilee, as the footnote notes and as Mark 1:39 has. Luke often uses Judea broadly for the land of the Jews, so the wider reading may simply mean the Jewish homeland.
